spec_match.rationale: Registers a real service worker, runs a genuine backgroundFetch.fetch() over three same-origin files, and reports per-record status/type/readability from the worker's backgroundfetchsuccess event — the baseline control the enforcement demos are measured against.

interactive.rationale: Start and Abort buttons, a live progress track, a step checklist, and a worker-reported record table; verified the run completes end-to-end with 3/3 records readable.

blurb_alignment.rationale: The card promises a real worker-reported download baseline and the page delivers exactly that.

edge_cases.rationale: Capability steps fail individually with reasons, a six-second zero-byte watchdog explains stalled headless/download-service environments honestly, and slow downloads get a distinct progressing message rather than a stuck bar.

references.rationale: Links https://chromestatus.com/feature/6210300985606144 and the Background Fetch specification.

conformance.rationale: The suite covers the manager, registration member, responseReady, secure context and a real opaque-vs-cors fetch pair, but its background-fetch-requires-user-activation assertion reads FAIL (not blocked) on any fresh profile because getRegistration() finds no service worker — flagged for a human, not edited.

runtime_evidence.rationale: Chromium 141 headless (cloud, no chrome-devtools-mcp): a trusted CDP click on Start produced a full success — worker registered, id accepted, progress reached 80,048/80,048 bytes, worker reported 3/3 records readable (200/default) — with a clean console and no failed same-origin requests; desktop 1280 and mobile 360 screenshots read.

telemetry_health.rationale: Loads demo-telemetry.js and emits background-fetch-reported/stalled/progressing asserts covering the success and degraded paths.

design_system.rationale: CSS variables throughout, button colour pair overridden together, progress bar and steps use accent variables, no static card.

accessibility.rationale: aria-live output for the result, captioned table with scoped headers, aria-hidden step icons with text equivalents, 44px buttons; the progress track also carries a text readout rather than colour alone.

mobile_desktop_parity.rationale: No horizontal overflow at 360x740 DPR3 (scrollWidth 360, screenshot read); table cells wrap via overflow-wrap:anywhere.

openQuestions.title: Make the Abort button actually exercisable
openQuestions.detail: On localhost the three files (~80KB) complete near-instantly, so the Abort branch is effectively unreachable and untested — the reviewer could not exercise it either. Consider adding a larger or server-throttled asset option (e.g. a /public route that streams slowly) so abort() and the backgroundfetchabort worker event can be demonstrated for real, which would also cover the cancellation anti-regression case.

summary: Reviewed at http://localhost:3000/v154/cors-enforcement-for-background-fetch/same-origin/ with Chromium 141 headless (cloud, no chrome-devtools-mcp). A CDP Input-domain click (trusted, grants user activation) ran the whole flow: all five capability steps green, fetch accepted, progress bar filled to 80,048 bytes, and the service worker reported backgroundfetchsuccess with 3/3 records readable. Console showed only intentional logs; the fonts.googleapis.com cert failure is a sandbox proxy artifact. Desktop 1280 and mobile 360 DPR3 screenshots read, no overflow. Feature /conformance/ ran 6 pass / 1 fail; the failing background-fetch-requires-user-activation assertion returns false on a fresh profile because no service worker registration exists yet — that reads as a spec failure when it is a missing-precondition state, flagged for human review (assertions are immutable). Only follow-up: the Abort path cannot realistically be exercised with such small local files.
